draft.title: Binary fission
card: Binary fission is how prokaryotes such as bacteria divide. One cell becomes two cells.
First the cell copies its circular DNA. The two copies attach to different parts of the cell membrane.
The cell then grows longer, which moves the two DNA copies apart. The membrane and cell wall grow inwards and split the cell in two.
The two new cells are genetically identical to the parent unless a mutation occurs. Fission can be fast: some bacteria divide about every 20 minutes in good conditions.
draft.remember: Binary fission: copy the DNA, move the copies apart, split into two identical cells.

a.q: Which of these happens during binary fission in a bacterium?
opts: The DNA is copied and the cell splits into two cells
The nucleus divides and the chromosomes line up
The cell splits first and then copies its DNA
Two cells join and mix their DNA to make a new cell
a.why: The DNA must be copied before the cell splits, so that each new cell gets a copy. Splitting first would leave one cell with no DNA. Bacteria have no nucleus, so no nuclear division occurs.
a.clue: Each new cell needs its own DNA before the cell splits.

b.q: Dev grows a bacterial culture in a warm lab. After many rounds of binary fission, the cells are checked. What is most likely to be true of them?
opts: They are genetically identical, apart from any mutations
They are all different, because the DNA is shuffled
They each carry half the DNA of the original cell
They each have a nucleus formed during division
b.why: Binary fission copies all the DNA, and each new cell gets a full copy. So the cells are identical unless a mutation occurs. Shuffling of DNA and halving of DNA do not happen in this process.
b.clue: Think about what is copied before the cell splits.

a.best: The DNA is copied and the cell splits into two cells

b.best: They are genetically identical, apart from any mutations

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedging qualifier ('apart from any mutations'). A test-wise student could pick it over the flat, absolute distractors without knowing the idea.

First the cell copies its circular DNA. The two copies attach to different parts of the cell membrane.
The cell then grows longer, which moves the two DNA copies apart. The membrane and cell wall grow inwards and split the cell in two.

Each new cell gets a full copy of the DNA, so they are genetically identical to the parent unless a mutation occurs. Fission can be fast: some bacteria divide about every 20 minutes in good conditions.
proposal.remember: Binary fission: copy the DNA, move the copies apart, split into two identical cells.

a.q: Which of these happens during binary fission in a bacterium?
opts: The DNA is copied and the cell splits into two cells
The nucleus divides and the chromosomes line up
The cell splits first and then copies its DNA
Two cells join and mix their DNA to make a new cell

a.clue: Each new cell needs its own DNA before the cell splits.

b.q: Dev grows a bacterial culture in a warm lab. Ignoring mutations, how does the DNA of the cells compare after many rounds of binary fission?
opts: Identical, because each cell gets a full copy of the DNA
Different, because the DNA is shuffled at each split
Half the DNA each, because the parent's DNA is shared out
Different, because two cells join and mix their DNA
b.why: The DNA is copied before each split, so every new cell gets a full, identical copy. The DNA is not shared out in halves, because copying comes first. No shuffling or joining of cells happens in binary fission.
b.clue: Think about what happens to the DNA before the cell splits.

a.best: The DNA is copied and the cell splits into two cells

b.best: Identical, because each cell gets a full copy of the DNA
